title: The Lookout
full_review:
"The Lookout" (Miramax/Spyglass) is a crime thriller more character-driven than usual for the genre. In fact, for the first 20 minutes, there is no indication of the bank heist that is to come. Instead we have a compelling character study about Chris Pratt (Joseph Gordon-Levitt), once a Midwestern town's golden-boy athlete, but now brain-damaged after a horrific car accident in which his daredevil driving resulted in the deaths of two of his friends.

Though he appears normal, Chris clearly has trouble doing the simplest things -- like opening a can of spaghetti -- and also relating socially to other people and keeping his now-chemically imbalanced hormones and emotions in check. His short-term memory is affected as well, and he must write down anything important in his notebook.

Working as a night bank janitor, Chris spends his off-hours with his blind roommate and empathetic mentor, the sardonic Lewis (Jeff Daniels in another fine character performance).

One night in a bar, Chris meets Gary Spargo (the versatile British actor Matthew Goode), a seemingly caring ruffian who prevents the bartender from cheating the vulnerable Chris, and more or less takes him under his wing. He also introduces Chris to the attractive Luvie Lemons (Isla Fisher), a former exotic dancer, who seduces the young man.

It soon develops that Spargo's true motivation in befriending Chris is to rob the bank where Chris works, with Chris playing lookout. Gary plays on Chris' frustrations at being in a dead-end job (the bank manager is reluctant to trust Chris with a teller position) and tells the reluctant young man they'll be taking the money not from the local farmers, but rather from the establishment. "Whoever has the money has the power" is Gary's mantra.

"The Lookout" shows us the sordid reality of criminal behavior. And it offers a redemptive message of how, paradoxically, letting go of the past and forgiving yourself can lead to the rediscovery of your true self.

All the performances are fine, with Gordon-Levitt particularly riveting in a difficult role.

The final third of the film is filled with numerous acts of violence, but writer and first-time director Scott Frank handles them -- and the brief sexual elements -- with relative restraint.

The film contains nongraphic premarital encounters, sexual innuendo and banter, violence including shootings and murder in self-defense, a brief violent car crash, fleeting rear nudity, skimpy female attire, drug and alcohol use, pervasive rough and crude language, crass expressions and some profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
